Baken
BAY-ken
verb (past participle)
The old strong past participle of bake, from the Old English bacan; retained by the Authorized Version where modern English has flattened it to baked — a word almost wholly given, in Scripture, to the offerings.

Biblical Definition

Baken is the Authorized Version’s old participle of bake, and it belongs chiefly to the altar. The meat offering — the bloodless offering of fine flour, oil, and frankincense — might be brought raw, or parched, or dressed in the pan or the fryingpan, or it might be “baken in the oven” (Lev 2:4), and then it was to be unleavened cakes of fine flour mingled with oil, or unleavened wafers anointed with oil. The rule is absolute: “It shall not be baken with leaven” (Lev 6:17), for it is most holy. Only at Pentecost does the law command the opposite — two wave loaves “baken with leaven” (Lev 23:17), the firstfruits of a harvest of sinners gathered into one church, still carrying what corruption remains in them and accepted only because the sacrifices are offered with them. The typology of the baken offering is plain. Fine flour is ground small and evenly, without a coarse grain in the whole measure; the oil is the anointing of the Spirit; the absence of leaven is the sinlessness of the offering; and the oven is the hidden fire, for a cake baken in the oven is baked out of sight, where no eye follows it. So was the humanity of Christ perfect and even-grained, anointed without measure, unleavened by any sin, and put into a fire whose worst heat no witness saw. There is one tender domestic use besides: the angel touched the exhausted Elijah, and “there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head” (1Ki 19:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

The old past participle of bake; used in the Authorized Version chiefly of the meat offering baken in the oven, and never with leaven.

expand to see more

BAKEN, the old participle passive of bake; dried, hardened, or dressed by heat in an oven or upon coals.

Old English bacan, whence bake, baker, batch.

The meat offering baken in the oven, of fine flour mingled with oil, unleavened (Lev 2:4).

It shall not be baken with leaven; it is most holy (Lev 6:17).

Excepted: the two Pentecost wave loaves, baken with leaven (Lev 23:17).

Key Scripture

Lev 2:4 — "And if thou bring an oblation of a meat offering baken in the oven, it shall be unleavened cakes of fine flour mingled with oil, or unleavened wafers anointed with oil."

Lev 6:17 — "It shall not be baken with leaven. I have given it unto them for their portion of my offerings made by fire; it is most holy, as is the sin offering, and as the trespass offering."

Lev 23:17 — "Ye shall bring out of your habitations two wave loaves of two tenth deals: they shall be of fine flour; they shall be baken with leaven; they are the firstfruits unto the LORD."

1Ki 19:6 — "And he looked, and, behold, there was a cake baken on the coals, and a cruse of water at his head. And he did eat and drink, and laid him down again."

Modern Corruption

No modern movement has redefined this old participle; the loss is that the baken offering is read as ritual detail rather than as a portrait of Christ under fire.

expand to see more

The neglect worth naming is not a redefinition but a habit of skipping. Leviticus 2 is where many a reading plan quietly dies, its ovens and pans and fryingpans dismissed as antique catering. Yet the Holy Ghost thought the manner of baking worth legislating, and the difference between the oven, the pan, and the fryingpan is the difference between a suffering wholly hidden, a suffering partly seen, and a suffering openly exposed — three views of one Christ, whose inward agony in Gethsemane and under the three hours’ darkness no eye beheld, while His outward affliction was seen of all. Fine flour speaks of a humanity with no unevenness, no knot, no coarse grain; leaven excluded speaks of a nature untouched by sin; oil mingled through the flour and poured upon it speaks of the Spirit’s anointing from the womb and at the Jordan; frankincense wholly burned speaks of a fragrance ascending to the Father which no man ever tasted. Read that way, the chapter is not tedious but adoring.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the ceremonial law is Christian doctrine in shadow, and that the shadows were drawn with deliberate exactness because the Body was exact. Nothing in the meat offering is accidental. Note too the single exception, for it guards against over-reading: at Pentecost the two wave loaves were baken with leaven (Lev 23:17), because there the offering is not Christ but the church — Jew and Gentile, two loaves and one feast, the firstfruits of the Spirit’s harvest, and leaven is in them still. They were never burned upon the altar; they were waved before the LORD, and accepted with the burnt offering and the sin offering that accompanied them. That is the gospel in a baking ordinance: the sinless One goes into the fire, and the leavened loaves are received for His sake. Finally, keep the cake baken on the coals for the fainting prophet under the juniper. The God who ordered the offerings also feeds His exhausted servants, and does not rebuke them first.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Authorized Version’s participle of bake; the offering passed through hidden fire, unleavened save at Pentecost.

expand to see more

Baken — old strong past participle of bake, Old English bacan.

Hebrew 'aphah, to bake; whence 'opheh, a baker.

Baken in the oven = hidden fire; in the pan and fryingpan = suffering more openly seen.

Unleavened and mingled with oil: sinless humanity anointed by the Spirit.

The one leavened exception is Pentecost’s two wave loaves — the church, not the Christ.

Usage

"Baken in the oven: the fire that no witness saw, which is Gethsemane and the darkness."

"It shall not be baken with leaven — the offering must be as sinless as the Offerer."

"Pentecost’s loaves are baken WITH leaven, for they are the church and not the Christ."
